newsitem.title: USA: Dornan seeks recount in U.S. congressional race.
newsitem.headline: Dornan seeks recount in U.S. congressional race.

text.p: Veteran Congressman Robert Dornan, an arch-conservative who blamed voter fraud for his narrow defeat by a political novice in last month's election, asked for a recount on Monday.

Dornan, a feisty Republican known as "B-1 Bob" because of his strong support for the military, wrote to Orange County Registrar of Voters Rosalyn Lever, "formally and respectfully" requesting a recount in the Nov. 5 election for California's 46th District.
Lever certified last week that Democratic businesswoman Loretta Sanchez, 36, had beaten Dornan by 984 votes, winning 47,964 votes to his 46,980.

Dornan, 63, asked Lever to begin the recount by looking at absentee ballots received after Nov. 3 and then to examine provisional votes cast on election day by people who had lost their absentee ballots or were voting at a different polling station than they were supposed to.

Dornan aide Pat Fanelli said an unusually high number of absentee ballots were cast. "There's room to believe there might be some problems there in the absentee ballots and the provisionals," she said.
Fanelli said the recount would begin next Monday but did not know how long it would take.

Lever was not available for comment and Sanchez's spokesman could not be reached. Sanchez, whose success was seen as a sign of the growing clout of Hispanic voters, long ago claimed victory in the race.
Dornan will have to pay for the recount at a cost of $358 per day for a four-member counting board.

Dornan has blamed voter fraud for his defeat, alleging non-citizens voted and that ballot boxes were not correctly sealed after the polls. After the elections, Dornan said: "I will not concede to an inarticulate, flaky, non-qualified person."

The defeat was a stinging blow to Dornan, seeking his 10th term in Congress, and a feather in the cap of Democrats, who picked up two other Republican-held congressional seats in California in last month's election.
The White House threw its support behind Sanchez's effort to oust the tough-talking congressman, who made a brief unsuccessful bid for the 1996 Republican presidential nomination.
Dornan, a former Air Force pilot, gained a reputation for strong opposition to abortion, communism, homosexual rights and gun control during his 18 years in Congress.
Sanchez, a financial analyst who had never held elected office, campaigned as a moderate while painting Dornan as an extremist out of step with the needs of his largely working-class constituents.
